parts.title: Joining a conservation group
parts.context: A man phones a conservation group to ask about volunteering.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a conservation group to ask about volunteering. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Greenway Conservation Volunteers, Ruth speaking.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Hi, my name's Sam. I've just moved to the area and I'd like to do some volunteering outdoors at weekends.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Wonderful. Let me tell you about this month's activities. On Saturday we're doing hedge laying.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The first activity is hedge laying, so 'hedge laying' has been written in the table. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Hedge laying? What does that involve?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: You cut the stems partly through and bend them over, so the hedge grows thicker and gives birds somewhere to nest. We meet in the car park at Holloway Farm. That's H-O-L-L-O-W-A-Y.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Got it. Do I need any special clothing?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Old clothes, and you'll definitely need a pair of thick gloves. The hawthorn has very sharp thorns. We lend out the tools, so you don't need to worry about those.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: And the pond clearing I saw on your website? Is that on Saturday too?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: The website says Saturday, but it's been moved to Sunday, because the farmer needs the field on Saturday. For that one we meet outside the village church, and you'll need boots, of course, wellingtons if you have them.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Fine. And is there anything for people who'd rather not get muddy?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: There's the bird survey, also on Sunday. That starts from the visitor centre. You walk a set route and count the birds you see. Bring a pair of binoculars if you have some. If not, we have a few you can borrow.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: That all sounds great. Is there an age limit? My son is fifteen and he's keen to come along.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: I'm afraid volunteers have to be at least sixteen, because of the tools we use. He'd be very welcome next year, though.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: OK. And how do people get there? I don't have a car at the moment.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: We run a minibus. It leaves from the station at half past eight, and it brings everyone back at about four.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: And what about food?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Bring your own packed lunch. We do provide hot soup at lunchtime, which is very welcome in winter. Tea and coffee too, of course.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Lovely. Is there any paperwork?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Just one form. You don't need any references, but for insurance reasons every volunteer has to fill in a health form before their first day, so we know about any medical conditions.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: No problem. Can I just turn up this weekend?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: New volunteers need to come to an induction day first, where we cover safety. The next one is on the third of March. I'll email you the details.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: The third of March. Great, thank you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Starting work at a hotel
parts.context: A hotel manager talks to new members of staff on their first day.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a hotel manager talking to new members of staff on their first day. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: claire
script.text: Good morning, and welcome to the Lakeside Hotel. I'm Claire, the general manager. Before we start the tour, take a look at the plan of the ground floor, because you'll be finding your way around it all day.

script.speaker: claire
script.text: We're standing at the main entrance, at the bottom of the plan. Reception is on your right as you come in, and the lifts are on your left.

script.speaker: claire
script.text: The first room you need to know is the staff room, because that's where your lockers are. Walk straight ahead from the entrance until you reach the corridor. Directly opposite you, on the other side of the corridor, is the staff room.

script.speaker: claire
script.text: Guests often arrive before their rooms are ready, so they leave their bags with us. The luggage room is just past reception, on the right, in the corner of the building. It's always kept locked, and the key is at the reception desk.

script.speaker: claire
script.text: Housekeeping staff will spend a lot of time in the laundry. To get there, turn left along the corridor and go all the way to the end, past the restaurant. The laundry is the last room at that end, on the left.

script.speaker: claire
script.text: My own office is at the other end. Turn right along the corridor, and it's the last door on the left, in the corner next to the fire exit. My door is always open, so come and find me if you have a problem.

script.speaker: claire
script.text: And finally, the gym. Guests ask about it all the time. It's just to the left of the lifts, so you can see it from the entrance, and it's open from six in the morning until ten at night.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: claire
script.text: Now, a few things about your shifts. You'll be able to check the rota online before you come in, so there's no need to look for it here. When you arrive, please don't sign in at reception. That used to be the system, but now you scan your staff card in the staff room. After that, pick up a radio from the charging station, so we can always reach you, and read the notice board, because there's always something new on it, like a large group arriving or a room out of use. You're welcome to arrive already in uniform if you prefer.

script.speaker: claire
script.text: As for benefits, meals during your shift are free, in the staff canteen behind the kitchen. I'm afraid the gym is for guests only, so staff can't use it. But you get thirty per cent off rooms for your friends and family, which is very popular. Parking isn't free, but there is a reduced rate in the hotel car park. And holidays are the standard amount for the first two years.

script.speaker: claire
script.text: Finally, complaints. Every hotel gets them. If a guest complains to you, please don't send them off to find a supervisor. Try to solve the problem yourself, there and then. You're allowed to offer a free drink or a later checkout, for example. Most guests just want to feel that someone is listening. Only call a supervisor if you really can't sort it out. Right, let's start the tour.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A presentation on bioplastics
parts.context: Two environmental science students discuss their presentation on bioplastics with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students, Jamal and Erin, discussing their presentation on bioplastics with their tutor, Dr Hughes. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: So, bioplastics. I seem to remember suggesting packaging as a topic. Was that what made you choose it?

script.speaker: erin
script.text: You did suggest packaging in general, and I'd read an article about plastic in the oceans. But what really decided it was Jamal's internship.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: Yes, I spent the summer at a company that makes food packaging, and they were testing plant-based plastics. So I already knew quite a lot, and I had contacts there.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Useful. How have you found the research?

script.speaker: erin
script.text: There's plenty of it, and most of it is recent, which is good. The problem is that a lot of what we found online was written by companies that make bioplastics, so of course it's very positive. We've had to look hard for independent studies.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: That's an important point to mention in the presentation itself. Now, I think the presentation would be more memorable with a case study. Something real and local.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: What about the café on campus? They switched to compostable cups last year.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Perfect. You could find out how it's gone.

script.speaker: erin
script.text: The other thing is length. We ran through it yesterday and it was nearly twenty-five minutes, and we only have fifteen.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Where could you save time?

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: The slides are fine, and the conclusion is already short. I think the history section is the obvious thing to cut. It's interesting, but it's not really what the presentation is about.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: I agree. So what's the plan for this week?

script.speaker: erin
script.text: I'll contact the café owner to ask if we can use them as our case study, and whether they'll share their figures.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Let's go through the materials you're covering. Start with PLA.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: PLA is made from corn starch, and it's probably the best-known bioplastic. But people think it just rots away in the garden, and it doesn't. It only breaks down in industrial composting plants, at high temperatures, and most towns don't have one.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: And the seaweed film?

script.speaker: erin
script.text: That's my favourite. It can even be eaten. But at the moment it costs about four times as much as ordinary plastic, so companies just won't pay for it.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: The packaging made from mushrooms?

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: That's grown from mushroom roots on farm waste. It's a lovely idea, but it's really still in the lab. Only a couple of small companies have tried it so far.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Sugarcane plastic?

script.speaker: erin
script.text: It performs very well, and it can be recycled with normal plastic. Our concern is that it uses crops grown on land that could produce food, which is a big issue in some countries.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: And finally, starch-based bags.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: Those are already everywhere. Most supermarkets in this country use them for fruit and vegetables, so the audience will know them.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Good. It sounds like you're in good shape.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how habits work
parts.context: A psychology lecture on how habits form and how they can be changed.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how habits form and how they can be changed. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today we're looking at habits: the things we do without thinking. Psychologists define a habit as a behavior that is performed automatically in response to a cue, such as a time of day, a place or a feeling.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Habits make up a surprisingly large part of our lives. One well-known study asked people to record what they were doing every hour, and found that forty-three per cent of their daily actions were habits, carried out while they were thinking about something else.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Researchers often describe a habit as a loop with three stages. First comes the cue. Then comes the routine, which is the behavior itself. And finally there's the reward, the pleasant feeling that makes the brain want to repeat the loop next time. Without a reward, a habit is very unlikely to form.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Brain scans show that as a behavior becomes a habit, activity moves away from the parts of the brain involved in decision-making, towards a deeper structure called the basal ganglia. This is why habits feel effortless, and also why they're so hard to stop.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So how long does it take to form a new habit? You may have heard that it takes twenty-one days, but there's no real evidence for that. When researchers in London followed volunteers trying to build new habits, the average was sixty-six days, although it varied enormously from person to person.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The same study had some encouraging news. Missing a single day made no real difference to whether the habit formed, so people don't need to give up after one slip. What did help was linking the new behavior to an existing habit. For example, someone who wants to floss their teeth might do it straight after brushing them, because brushing acts as the cue.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Breaking a bad habit is harder. Willpower alone rarely works, because the habit is triggered automatically. A more effective approach is to change the environment where the habit happens. People who move house, for example, often find it easier to give up smoking, because the old cues are gone.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Another strategy is to add friction, that is, to make the unwanted behavior less convenient. Putting your phone in another room at night is a simple example. Even a few extra seconds of effort can be enough to break the automatic chain.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, we shouldn't forget that habits are social. Studies have found that people are more likely to take up exercise, or to give up smoking, if others in their social network do the same. So one of the best ways to change a habit may be to change who we spend our time with.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
